_about: Every series the site can show. Pages pick from these by name in their LAYOUT. python/build_data.py fetches everything listed here into data/macro.json.

RealGDP.label: Real GDP
RealGDP.desc: Inflation-adjusted value of everything the US produces, in chained 2017 dollars, published quarterly by the BEA; the tile shows growth over the past year. Trend growth is roughly 2% a year. Two negative quarters is a popular recession rule of thumb, but the NBER's official dating looks at a wider set of indicators. Each quarter is estimated three times and revised later.

RetailSales.label: Retail Sales
RetailSales.desc: Dollar value of goods sold by retailers and restaurants each month, from the Census Bureau about two weeks after month end. Consumer spending is roughly two-thirds of GDP, so this is the earliest broad read on it. Caveat: it is not adjusted for inflation, so compare it with CPI, since higher prices alone lift sales. Often revised.

Unemployment.label: Unemployment Rate
Unemployment.desc: Share of the labor force without a job that looked for work in the past four weeks, from the BLS household survey, usually released the first Friday of the month. Around 4% has marked a tight labor market; maximum employment is half the Fed's mandate. A sustained rise of about half a point has historically signaled recession (see the Sahm rule).

U6.label: Underemployment (U-6)
U6.desc: The broadest unemployment measure: the official rate plus people who want work but stopped looking recently, and part-timers who want full-time hours. It runs several points above the headline rate. A gap that widens between the two points to underemployment that the headline number misses. Same BLS household survey and release as the unemployment rate.

PrimeEPOP.label: Prime-Age Employment Rate (25–54)
PrimeEPOP.desc: Share of Americans aged 25 to 54 who have a job, from the BLS household survey. Many economists prefer it to the unemployment rate because it isn't distorted by people who stop looking for work or by an aging population retiring. Higher is stronger; around 80% has historically marked a very strong labor market.

Payrolls.label: Nonfarm Payrolls
Payrolls.desc: Number of jobs on employer payrolls, excluding farms, private households and the self-employed, from the BLS establishment survey (the 'jobs report'). The headline is the monthly change. Estimates of the gain needed to keep pace with population growth range from roughly 50k to 150k a month, depending on immigration. Revised in each of the next two months, plus an annual benchmark.

JoblessClaims.label: Initial Jobless Claims
JoblessClaims.desc: First-time claims for state unemployment benefits, published every Thursday for the prior week. It is the most timely labor indicator and rises quickly as layoffs pick up. Weekly numbers are noisy, so watch the trend over several weeks. Expansions typically run around 200–250k; claims topped 6 million in a single week in 2020.

ContClaims.label: Continuing Claims
ContClaims.desc: Number of people still receiving state unemployment benefits, published weekly with a one-week lag behind initial claims. Rising continuing claims while initial claims stay steady means people are taking longer to find new jobs, an early sign of a cooling labor market. Benefits usually end after about 26 weeks, so long spells drop out of the count.

SahmRule.label: Sahm Rule Recession Indicator
SahmRule.desc: The Sahm rule, developed by economist Claudia Sahm, compares the three-month average unemployment rate with its lowest three-month average over the prior 12 months. A reading of 0.50 points or more has historically meant a recession had already begun; near zero means unemployment is near its recent low. This real-time version uses data as first published, not later revisions.

JOLTS.label: Job Openings (JOLTS)
JOLTS.desc: Unfilled job openings on the last business day of the month, from the BLS JOLTS survey, released about five weeks later. Higher means stronger demand for workers. Openings per unemployed person peaked near 2 to 1 in 2022, a ratio Fed Chair Powell repeatedly highlighted as a sign of an overheated job market. Low response rates mean sizable revisions.

QuitRate.label: Quits Rate
QuitRate.desc: Share of workers who voluntarily quit their job during the month, from BLS JOLTS. People quit when they're confident they can find something better, so a high rate signals worker bargaining power and tends to lead faster wage growth; it hit records near 3% in 2021–22. A falling quit rate is an early sign the job market is cooling.

AHE.label: Average Hourly Earnings
AHE.desc: Average hourly pay of private-sector employees, from the BLS jobs report; the tile shows growth over the past year. Analysts often treat roughly 3–3.5% as consistent with 2% inflation given productivity growth, a rule of thumb rather than a Fed target. Caveat: shifts in who is employed (e.g. low-wage layoffs) can distort it; the ECI and Atlanta Fed tracker avoid this.

CorePCE.label: Core PCE Prices
CorePCE.desc: Price index for personal consumption expenditures excluding food and energy, from the BEA, monthly. The Fed's 2% target is defined on headline PCE, but it treats core as the best guide to where inflation is heading, because food and energy prices swing widely. Released after CPI and PPI, so the number is usually well anticipated.

PCE.label: PCE Prices
PCE.desc: Price index for everything households consume, from the BEA, monthly; this is the measure the Fed's 2% inflation target refers to. It is broader than CPI (it includes spending made on people's behalf, like employer-paid health care), adjusts its weights as buying habits change, and gives housing less weight, so it usually runs a few tenths below CPI.

CoreCPI.label: Core CPI
CoreCPI.desc: Consumer prices excluding food and energy, from the BLS, released mid-month. It shows the underlying trend without volatile food and gas prices. Shelter makes up roughly 40% or more of core CPI, so rents drive much of it. The 2% line is a reference only; the Fed's target is defined on PCE, which typically runs a bit lower.

CPI.label: Consumer Price Index (CPI)
CPI.desc: Prices of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by urban consumers, from the BLS, released mid-month. It is the most quoted inflation measure and is used to adjust Social Security and TIPS. The Fed's 2% target is on PCE, which usually runs a few tenths lower. CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, the highest since 1981.

ShelterCPI.label: CPI: Shelter
ShelterCPI.desc: The shelter part of CPI: rent plus owners' equivalent rent (OER), which estimates what homeowners would pay to rent their own home, based on rents and not home prices. It is about a third of the CPI basket. Because leases renew roughly once a year, it lags market rents by about a year, which is why it moves slowly.

Breakeven5.label: 5-Year Breakeven Inflation
Breakeven5.desc: The bond market's expected average inflation over the next five years: the 5-year Treasury yield minus the 5-year TIPS yield (e.g. 4.5% − 2.0% = 2.5%). Caveat: it also contains liquidity and risk premiums, and it tracks CPI, which runs above PCE, so readings around 2.3–2.5% are consistent with the Fed's 2% PCE target.

FedFunds.label: Fed Funds Rate
FedFunds.desc: Interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves. The Fed's FOMC sets a target range at eight scheduled meetings a year and keeps the rate inside it mainly by setting the interest it pays on reserves. It anchors all short-term borrowing costs: higher means tighter policy. Shown here as the monthly average effective rate.

Yield2Y.label: 2-Year Treasury Yield
Yield2Y.desc: Yield on the 2-year Treasury note, daily. It closely tracks where markets expect the Fed's policy rate to be over the next two years. Well below the fed funds rate means markets expect cuts; above it means hikes or rates staying high. It reacts quickly to jobs and inflation data.

Yield10Y.label: 10-Year Treasury Yield
Yield10Y.desc: Yield on the 10-year Treasury note, daily: the benchmark long-term interest rate. Mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs move with it. It reflects expected future short-term rates plus a term premium for holding long debt. Rising yields tighten financial conditions and tend to weigh on stocks and housing.

Spread.label: Yield Curve (10Y – 2Y)
Spread.desc: The 10-year Treasury yield minus the 2-year, daily. When it turns negative (an 'inverted' curve), markets expect rate cuts or weak growth ahead. Inversions preceded every US recession since the late 1960s, typically by 6 to 24 months. Caveat: the long 2022–24 inversion was not followed by a recession right away, so treat it as a warning, not a guarantee.

CreditSpread.label: Corporate Credit Spread (Baa – 10Y)
CreditSpread.desc: Extra yield investors demand to hold Moody's Baa-rated corporate bonds (the lowest investment grade) instead of 10-year Treasuries, daily. It widens when lenders worry about defaults and narrows when credit is easy. It peaked near 6 percentage points in the 2008 crisis; readings around 2 or below indicate easy credit conditions.

Mortgage30.label: 30-Year Mortgage Rate
Mortgage30.desc: Average 30-year fixed mortgage rate from Freddie Mac's weekly survey. It moves with the 10-year Treasury yield plus a spread. Example: going from 3% to 7% adds roughly $1,000 a month to the payment on a $400k loan. Owners with low locked-in rates are reluctant to sell (the 'lock-in effect'), which holds down supply.

CaseShiller.label: Home Prices (Case-Shiller National)
CaseShiller.desc: The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller National Home Price Index, tracking repeat sales of the same homes so changes in the mix of houses sold don't skew it. It is a 3-month moving average released with about a two-month lag; the tile shows the change over the past year. Home prices don't enter CPI directly; housing enters through rents.

Permits.label: Building Permits
Permits.desc: New housing units authorized by building permits, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, from the Census Bureau, monthly. Permits come before construction starts by a few months, so they are one of the best leading indicators for housing, and a component of the Conference Board's Leading Economic Index. Volatile month to month; watch the trend.

Starts.label: Housing Starts
Starts.desc: New housing units on which construction began, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, from the Census Bureau, monthly. Very sensitive to mortgage rates, and construction has ripple effects on jobs and spending on materials and furnishings. Volatile, especially apartments, and revised, so the multi-month trend matters more than a single month.

NewHomeSales.label: New Home Sales
NewHomeSales.desc: New single-family home sales, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate in thousands, from the Census Bureau, monthly. A sale is counted when the contract is signed, so it reacts quickly to mortgage rates and is one of the earliest reads on housing demand. New homes are only about 10–15% of all sales; wide error margins and large revisions.

MonthsSupply.label: Months' Supply of New Homes
MonthsSupply.desc: How many months the current inventory of new homes for sale would last at the current sales pace, from Census new residential sales data; it includes homes not yet built. Around six months is usually considered balanced; well above that points to weak demand and pressure on builders to cut prices or offer incentives.

Supercore.label: Supercore PCE (Services ex-Housing)
Supercore.desc: PCE prices for services excluding energy and housing, often called supercore inflation. It covers labor-heavy services such as health care, restaurants, transportation and financial services, where wages drive prices. Fed Chair Powell singled it out in 2022–23 as key to the inflation outlook. The tile shows the change over the past year.

TrimmedPCE.label: Trimmed-Mean PCE (Dallas Fed)
TrimmedPCE.desc: The Dallas Fed trimmed-mean PCE inflation rate, 12-month. Each month it drops the most extreme price changes (roughly the lowest quarter and highest third by spending weight) and averages the rest. Filtering out one-off swings makes it a good guide to the underlying trend; the 2% line is the Fed's target.

PPIFinal.label: Producer Prices (Final Demand)
PPIFinal.desc: The headline Producer Price Index: prices businesses receive for goods, services and construction sold to final buyers, from the BLS, monthly. It can lead consumer inflation, and pieces such as medical services and airfares feed directly into PCE estimates. It is more volatile than consumer prices; the tile shows the change over the past year.

Fwd5y5y.label: 5y5y Forward Inflation Expectations
Fwd5y5y.desc: Expected average inflation over the five years starting five years from now, derived from 5- and 10-year Treasury and TIPS yields. Because it looks past the near term, the Fed uses it to judge whether long-run expectations stay anchored. Roughly 2–2.5% (on a CPI basis) is consistent with anchored expectations; also contains risk premiums.

MichExp.label: Consumer Inflation Expectations (1-yr)
MichExp.desc: Households' median expected inflation over the next 12 months, from the University of Michigan consumer survey, monthly. Expectations can feed into wage demands and pricing, which is why the Fed tracks them. Answers react strongly to gas and grocery prices and usually sit above actual inflation, so the trend matters more than the level. FRED posts it about a month late.

ECI.label: Employment Cost Index
ECI.desc: Cost of wages and benefits for a fixed mix of jobs, published quarterly by the BLS, so shifts in who is working don't skew it. It is the labor-cost measure the Fed watches most closely. Growth of roughly 3.5% or less a year is generally seen as consistent with 2% inflation. Quarterly, so it is slower than monthly wage data.

WageTracker.label: Wage Growth Tracker (Atlanta Fed)
WageTracker.desc: The Atlanta Fed wage growth tracker: the median 12-month pay change for the same individuals, smoothed as a 12-month average. Following the same people avoids the composition effects that distort average hourly earnings. It runs above other wage measures because individuals' pay rises with experience, so compare it with its own history.

Listings.label: Active Home Listings
Listings.desc: Number of homes actively listed for sale nationwide, from Realtor.com, monthly since 2016. Inventory is the key supply measure: low listings keep prices high even when sales are slow, and rising listings point to easing prices. Not seasonally adjusted, since listings rise every spring, so compare with the same month a year earlier.

NewHomePrice.label: Median New-Home Price
NewHomePrice.desc: Median sales price of new houses sold in the US, from the Census Bureau, quarterly. Caveat: it shifts with the mix of homes builders sell; a move toward smaller or cheaper homes can lower the median even if prices aren't falling. For the trend in home values, Case-Shiller is the better guide.

RealYield10Y.label: 10-Year Real Yield (TIPS)
RealYield10Y.desc: Yield on 10-year Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), daily: the real return investors require after inflation. Higher real yields tighten financial conditions and weigh on housing, stocks and gold. Roughly, the nominal 10-year yield equals this real yield plus expected inflation (the breakeven rate).

FinConditions.label: Financial Conditions (Chicago Fed)
FinConditions.desc: The Chicago Fed's National Financial Conditions Index, weekly, combining 105 measures of risk, credit and leverage. Zero is the historical average; negative means looser-than-average conditions, positive means tighter. It spiked in 2008 and March 2020. Small moves around zero matter less than the direction and sharp jumps.

SP500.label: S&P 500
SP500.desc: The S&P 500: 500 of the largest US companies, weighted by market value, from market prices. It is the standard benchmark for US stocks and is forward-looking, often turning before the economy does. Shown as price only, without dividends. The full-history chart uses a log scale so equal percentage moves look the same size across decades.

VIX.label: VIX Volatility Index
VIX.desc: The VIX: the 30-day volatility S&P 500 options are pricing in, often called the fear gauge. Readings below about 15 indicate calm markets; above 30 indicates stress. It spiked above 80 in 2008 and March 2020. It measures expected swings in either direction, not a forecast that stocks will fall.

Dollar.label: Broad Dollar Index
Dollar.desc: The Federal Reserve's nominal broad dollar index: the dollar against the currencies of 26 major trading partners, weighted by trade, including China, Mexico, Canada and the euro area (January 2006 = 100), daily. A stronger dollar makes imports cheaper and US exports pricier, and tightens global financial conditions because much of the world borrows in dollars. Not adjusted for inflation; history starts in 2006.

Oil.label: WTI Crude Oil
Oil.desc: West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude oil spot price at Cushing, Oklahoma, in dollars per barrel, daily from the US Energy Information Administration; shown as month-end values. Oil feeds directly into gasoline and transport costs, so big moves show up quickly in headline inflation. Price spikes preceded several past recessions. Prices are driven mainly by OPEC+ supply decisions and global demand, not the US economy alone.

Gold.label: Gold
Gold.desc: Gold futures, front month, in dollars per troy ounce. Gold tends to rise when real interest rates fall and when investors seek safety; central-bank buying has also been a large driver. Often called an inflation hedge, it holds value over long periods but can swing widely for years at a time.

Homebuilders.label: Homebuilders (ITB)
Homebuilders.desc: The iShares US Home Construction ETF, from market prices. It holds mostly large homebuilders plus building-product and supply companies. Builders' share prices tend to anticipate turns in housing activity months before the official data, though they also move with the broader stock market.
